1.title: The Big Day

story.title: Gulu and the Great Forest Race
story.content:
Little Gulu the squirrel sat at the edge of the Giant Park. Warm morning light lay on the grass like a golden blanket. Today was the day of the Great Forest Race, and everything felt very, very big.

Gulu saw the fast deer stretching their legs and the strong bears warming up near the old banyan tree. Families chattered. Leaves rustled. His heart went thump-thump inside his chest, like a tiny drum only he could hear.

"Too small for this," whispered a worried voice in his head.

His friend Kaka the crow called from a low branch, "You came! Good. But don't just stare—run when the horn blows!"

Gulu's paws wanted to hide. Instead, he remembered what Grandmother Owl had told him last night, reading from the old Gita story: even blind King Dhritarashtra could not see the field, but he asked his friend Sanjaya, "What is happening on the Field of Truth?" The king did not rush. He wanted to understand the scene before the big day truly began.

"So watching is allowed?" Gulu had asked.

"Watching is wise," Grandmother Owl had answered.

Gulu stood on his tiptoes and looked carefully. He saw where the path turned muddy. He saw where the deer would leap. He saw where the bears took wide steps. He noticed a narrow line of dry moss along the fence—small, but perfect for quick paws.

At the starting line, animals crowded and pushed. Gulu did not push back. He breathed in... and out... and watched, just like Prince Duryodhana in the next part of the story, who looked at the whole army before saying a single word to his teacher.

The horn blew. Deer shot forward like arrows. Bears thundered. Gulu waited one heartbeat—not from fear, but from quiet courage. Then he ran along the moss path his eyes had found.

Halfway through, he stumbled on a root. Kaka cawed, "Get up!" Gulu paused, looked at the root, looked at the finish hill, and ran again. The butterflies in his tummy did not vanish—they changed. They felt less like heavy clouds and more like brave sparks lighting his way.

Gulu did not win first place. The deer did. But Gulu crossed the finish line with his chest lifted, paws muddy, eyes bright. The forest cheered not only for the fastest, but for the small squirrel who had watched first, chosen his path, and run with a joyful, determined heart.

Quiet courage, Gulu learned, is not the loudest roar. It is the steady choice to see clearly—and then take one brave step.
story.content_te:
చిన్న అడవి ఉడుత గులు పెద్ద పార్క్ అంచున కూర్చున్నాడు. ఉదయం వెచ్చని సూర్యకాంతి పచ్చ గడ్డి మీద బంగారు దుప్పటి లా పడి ఉంది. ఈ రోజు గొప్ప అడవి పరుగు — అన్నీ చాలా, చాలా పెద్దగా అనిపించాయి.

వేగమైన జింకలు కాళ్లు విస్తరించుకుంటున్నాయి. బలమైన ఎలుగుబంట్లు పాత మర్రి చెట్టు దగ్గర సాధన చేస్తున్నాయి. కుటుంబాలు మాట్లాడుకుంటున్నాయి. ఆకులు చపచప మఱిపిస్తున్నాయి. గులు గుండె thump-thump అని కొట్టుకుంది — అతనికే వినిపించే చిన్న డ్రమ్ లా.

"ఇది నాకు చాలా పెద్దది," అని మనస్సులో ఒక చింతిత గొంతు గుసగుసలాడింది.

అతని స్నేహితుడు కాకి కాకా తక్కువ కొమ్మ నుండి అన్నాడు, "వచ్చావ! బాగుంది. కానీ చూస్తూనే ఉండకు — బాక ఊదినప్పుడు పరుగెత్తు!"

గులు పాదాలు దాక్కుకోవాలని అనిపించాయి. కానీ రాత్రి అజ్జమ్మ గedu పitta గీతా కథ చెప్పింది గుర్తు వచ్చింది: అంధుడైన ధృతరాష్ట్ర రాజు మైదానం చూడలేకపోయినా, తన స్నేహితుడు సంజయను అడిగాడు — "ధర్మ క్షేత్రంలో ఏమి జరుగుతోంది?" రాజు తొందరపెట్టలేదు. పెద్ద రోజు నిజంగా మొదలవ్వడానికి ముందు పరిస్థితిని అర్థం చేసుకోవాలని అనుకున్నాడు.

"అంటే చూడడం సరైనదా?" గులు అడిగాడు.

"చూడడం తెలివైనది," అజ్జమ్మ గedu పitta అన్నది.

గులు అడుగుల మీద ఎత్తి జాగ్రత్తగా చూశాడు. ఎక్కడ మట్టి ముదురుగా ఉందో, జింకలు ఎక్కడ దూకుతారో, ఎలుగుబంట్లు ఎక్కడ విస్తృత అడుగులు వేస్తారో చూశాడు. కంచె పక్కన పొడి moss బాగా ఇరుకైన మార్గం — చిన్న పాదాలకు అద్భుతం.

స్టార్ట్ లైన్‌లో జంతువులు నెట్టుకుంటున్నారు. గులు తిరిగి నెట్టలేదు. శ్వాస తీసుకున్నాడు... వదిలాడు... చూశాడు — కథలోని తదుపరి భాగంలో రాకుమారుడు దుర్యోధనుడు గురువుకు ఒక్క మాట మాట్లాడకముందే మొత్తం సైన్యాన్ని చూశాడు.

బాక ఊదింది. జింకలు బాణాల లా ముందుకు దూసుకుపోయాయి. ఎలుగుబంట్లు గర్జించాయి. గులు ఒక గుండె కొట్టుకునే క్షణం వేచి ఉన్నాడు — భయం కాదు, నిశ్శబ్ద ధైర్యం. తర్వాత కళ్లు కనుగొన్న moss మార్గంలో పరిగెత్తాడు.

మధ్యలో ఒక వేరు మీద జారిపడాడు. కాకా "లే!" అని అరిచింది. గులు ఆగి, వేరు చూశాడు, ముగింపు కొండ చూశాడు, మళ్లీ పరిగెత్తాడు. కడుపulo సీతాకోక చిలukalu అగిపోle da — avi maaraayi. Bhari meghala la kaadu, dhairyamaina merupula laga anipinchaayi.

మొదటి sthanam raadu. Jinka gelichindi. Kaani Gulu finish line daati tana chati ettukoni, paadalu drushthi thota mud tho, kallu merisinavi. Adavi vegamaina vaarikosam kuda, mundu chusi, tana daari emchukoni, santoshamga mariyu drudha hrudayam tho parigettina chinna squirrel kosam kuda jai jai annaru.

Nishshabda dhairyam ante pedda garjan kaadu ani Gulu nerchukunnadu. Spashtamga chusi, taruvaata oka dhairyamaina adugu veyadam.
story.moral: Quiet courage begins when you watch carefully, understand the scene, and then take one brave step—even if your heart goes thump-thump.

1.title: The Inner Brave

story.title: Gulu and the Crossroad
story.content:
The Great Forest Race had started, but Gulu the squirrel reached a place where the path split in two. One path was bright with morning sun. One path was shadowy and cool. Gulu gripped his lucky twig like a tiny bow. "Which way is the right way?" he wondered.

Above him, a small leaf flag with a monkey symbol fluttered in the breeze. It reminded Gulu of the brave stories of Hanuman. Gulu stood a little taller. His chest felt warm, like he was finding his inner brave.

Grandmother Owl landed softly on a low branch. "Don't just pick a side because you're in a hurry, Gulu," she hooted. "A true leader looks at everything first."

"Can we go to the very middle?" Gulu asked. He wanted to see the bright path and the shadowy path at the same time. He wanted to be a Middle-Seeker.

Grandmother Owl nodded. Together they walked to the center of the crossroad. The forest was noisy there. Some animals shouted, "Go left!" Others shouted, "Go right!" Gulu did not shout. He just stood still and listened.

Standing in the middle was like having a secret window. Gulu looked left and saw sharp thorns hiding in the grass. He looked right and saw a path that was very slippery after the rain. Both sides looked tricky.

Because he stayed in the middle, Gulu saw something no one else saw. Right between the two noisy paths was a secret trail of soft, green moss—gentle, safe, and perfect for small paws.

"Look!" Gulu called out. By standing his ground in the middle, he had found the safest way for everyone. The other animals stopped shouting and looked at Gulu with wide eyes.

Gulu did not just run ahead alone. He led. He picked up his twig-bow and stepped onto the moss. He wasn't afraid of the paths anymore because he had seen them both clearly.

"I found my Inner Brave," Gulu whispered. Grandmother Owl winked. Taking the lead wasn't about being first—it was about finding the truth for everyone.

Gulu remembered the Gita story Grandmother Owl had told him: brave Arjuna, with Hanuman on his flag, lifted his bow when the challenge began. Then he asked Krishna to stop the chariot in the middle of the field so he could see everyone clearly before choosing. That was the same kind of brave—standing in the middle to see the whole picture.
story.content_te:
గొప్ప అడవి పరుగu మొదలైందi, కానీ ఉడుత గులu రెండు దారులu విడిపోయే చోటu చేరాడు. ఒక దారi morning sun tho merisindi. maro daari nillala cool ga undi. Gulu tana lucky twig ni chinna bow la pattukunnadu. "E daari correct?" ani alochinchadu.

Paina oka leaf flag lo monkey symbol gali lo egurutundi. Hanuman goppa kathalu gurtu vachayi. Gulu konchem ettu ga nilichadu — lopala dhairyam kanipinchindi.

Grandmother Owl mriduvuga branch meeda digindi. "Toraga oka vippu emchuko, Gulu," ani hoot chesindi. "Nijamaina leader mundu anni chustadu."

"Madhyalo vellochema?" Gulu adigadu. Bright path kooda, shadow path kooda okesari chudali anukunnadu. Middle-Seeker avvali.

Owl talavunindi. Crossroad madhyalo vellaru. Adavi chala noisy. Konni jantuvulu "Left!" ani arustunnayi. Inkondaru "Right!" ani. Gulu aravale. Nishabdamga vinadu.

Madhyalo nilabadatam secret window la. Left lo sharp thorns kanipinchaayi. Right lo slippery path. Rendu tricky.

Madhyalo undi Gulu vere evvaru choodani vishayam chusaadu — rendu noisy paths madhya soft green moss trail!

"Chudandi!" Gulu pilichadu. Madhyalo nilabadi andariki safe daari kanipettadu. Jantuvulu aagipoyi chusaru.

Gulu okkade parigettale — lead chesadu. Twig-bow pattukoni moss meeda adug vesadu. Rendu daarulu clear ga chusaka bhayam ledu.

"Na Inner Brave kanipettanu," Gulu gusagusa. Owl kindiki kindiki chusi. Lead ante first kaadu — truth kanipettadam andariki.

Gulu Gita katha gurtu chesukunnadu: Arjuna, Hanuman flag tho, challenge modata bow ettuadu. Taruvata Krishna ni madhyalo ratham aapamani adigadu — rendu sides clear ga chusi emchukovadaniki. Ade brave — middle lo nilabadi whole picture choodatam.
story.moral: A brave heart stands in the middle to see the truth. When you see the whole picture, you can lead with fairness and wisdom.

story.title: Aarav and the Republic Day Rehearsal
story.content:
Aarav loved Tuesdays at Greenfield School because they meant games period. But this Tuesday was different. The whole school was rehearsing for Republic Day, and the playground had turned into a parade ground.

When Aarav walked through the main gate, a deep drum sound rolled across the field—dum, dum, dum-dum! The school band was practicing. Trumpets blared. A teacher clapped a steady beat with wooden sticks. Even the little children on the veranda pressed their palms over their ears and giggled.

Aarav's heart jumped like a cricket in a lunch box. His palms felt sweaty inside his blue uniform.

"Too loud?" asked his classmate Priya, shouting over the music.

"My heart is running a race," Aarav admitted.

Priya nodded. "Mine too. But watch—nobody is running away."

She was right. The flag-bearers stood tall. The karate team held its stance. The drum players breathed in, then struck again. The sound was huge, but it was not a scary sound—not like shouting in anger. It was the sound of a big day waking up.

At home that night, Aarav told his grandmother about the rehearsal while she strung jasmine flowers on the porch.

Nani smiled. "In the Gita story, when a great day began on a wide field, conch shells and drums sounded together. The noise was so loud that hearts beat faster in many chests—even brave ones. The sound did not mean danger. It meant something important was starting, and everyone had to listen with their whole body."

Aarav's eyes grew wide. "So fast hearts can be normal?"

"Yes," Nani said. "Loud moments wake the body before the mind catches up. Breathe slowly. Let your feet feel the ground."

The next rehearsal was still loud. Dum-dum went the drums. The trumpets sang. Aarav pressed his hand to his chest and counted four slow breaths, the way Nani had taught him. In... out... in... out.

He watched the flag rise in practice. He watched his teacher's calm face. His heart still beat quickly, but his legs stopped wobbling. When the band finished, the playground fell quiet for one second—and Aarav laughed with relief.

On Republic Day morning, the drums returned, louder than ever. Aarav's heart drummed along. This time he marched with his class, chin up, ears awake, and feet steady on the red ground. The loud moment did not shrink him. It reminded him that big days can make the whole school—and the whole heart—come alive together.

ఆరవ్‌కు గ్రీన్‌ఫీల్డ్ పాఠశాలలో మంగళవారాలు ఇష్టం — ఆటల కాలం అంటే. కానీ ఈ మంగళవారం వేరు. మొత్తం పాఠశాల రిపబ్లిక్ డే కోసం రిహర్సల్ చేస్తోంది, ఆట మైదానం పరేడ్ గ్రౌండ్‌గా మారింది.

ఆరవ్ ప్రధాన గేట్ దాటి వెళ్లగానే లోతైన డ్రమ్ ధ్వని మైదానం మొత్తం మీదుగా గుడిగింది — డమ్, డమ్, డమ్-డమ్! పాఠశాల బ్యాండ్ సాధన చేస్తోంది. ట్రంపెట్లు మ్రోగాయి. ఒక ఉపాధ్యాయుడు చెక్క కర్రలతో స్థిరమైన బీట్ కొట్టాడు. వరండాలో చిన్న పిల్లలు కూడా చెవులు మూసుకుని నవ్వారు.

ఆరవ్ గుండె లంచ్ బాక్స్‌లోని గ్రికెట్ లాగా దూకింది. నీలం యూనిఫారంలో చేతులు చెమటతో తడిసిపోయాయి.

"చాలా బిగ్గరగా ఉందా?" అతని సహపాఠిని ప్రియ అని అరుస్తూ అడిగింది.

"నా గుండె పరుగు పందెం పడుతోంది," ఆరవ్ అంగీకరించాడు.

"నాది కూడా," ప్రియ తల వూనింది. "కానీ చూడు — ఎవరూ పారిపోవడం లేదు."

ఆమె చెప్పింది నిజం. జండా ఎత్తిన వారు నిటారుగా నిల్చారు. కరాటే జట్టు స్థితి పట్టుకుంది. డ్రమ్ వాయించే వారు శ్వాస తీసుకుని మళ్లీ కొట్టారు. ధ్వని భారీగా ఉంది, కానీ భయంకరమైనది కాదు — కోపంతో అరుపులా కాదు. పెద్ద రోజు మేల్కొన్న ధ్వని.

ఆ రాత్రి ఇంట్లో ఆరవ్ తన అమ్మమ్మకు రిహర్సల్ గురించి చెప్పాడు. ఆమె తావేడిపై మల్లె పూలు కలుపుతూ విన్నారు.

నాని నవ్వింది. "గీతా కథలో విశాలమైన మైదానంలో గొప్ప రోజు మొదలైనప్పుడు శంఖాలు, డ్రమ్స్ కలిసి మ్రోగాయి. ధ్వని చాలా బిగ్గరగా ఉండి చాలా మంది ఛాతీల్లో గుండెలు త్వరగా కొట్టాయి — ధైర్యవంతులది కూడా. ఆ ధ్వనికి ప్రమాదం అర్థం కాదు. ముఖ్యమైనది మొదలవుతోందని, అందరూ మొత్తం శరీరంతో వినాలని అర్థం."

"త్వరగా కొట్టే గుండెలు సాధారణమా?" ఆరవ్ కళ్లు పెద్దవయ్యాయి.

"అవును," నాని అన్నారు. "బిగ్గర క్షణాలు మనస్సు గమనించే ముందు శరీరాన్ని మేల్కొల్పుతాయి. నెమ్మదిగా శ్వాస తీసుకో. పాదాలు నేలను అనుభవించనివ్వు."

తదుపరి రిహర్సల్ కూడా బిగ్గరగానే ఉంది. డమ్-డమ్ డ్రమ్స్. ట్రంపెట్లు పాడాయి. ఆరవ్ చేతిని ఛాతిపై ఉంచి నాని నేర్పినట్లు నాలుగు నెమ్మది శ్వాసలు లెక్కించాడు. లోపలికి... బయటకు... లోపలికి... బయటకు.

అభ్యాసంలో జండా ఎత్తడం చూశాడు. ఉపాధ్యాయుని ప్రశాంత ముఖం చూశాడు. గుండె ఇంకా త్వరగా కొట్టింది, కానీ కాళ్లు వణికడం ఆగింది. బ్యాండ్ ముగిసినప్పుడు మైదానం ఒక క్షణం నిశ్శబ్దమైంది — ఆరవ్ ఉపశమనంతో నవ్వాడు.

రిపబ్లిక్ డే ఉదయం డ్రమ్స్ తిరిగి వచ్చాయి, మునుపటి కంటే బిగ్గరగా. ఆరవ్ గుండె కూడా డ్రమ్ అయింది. ఈసారి తన తరగతితో నడిచాడు, తల ఎత్తి, చెవులు మేల్కొని, ఎరుపు నేలపై పాదాలు స్థిరంగా. బిగ్గర క్షణం అతన్ని చిన్నదిగా చేయలేదు. పెద్ద రోజు మొత్తం పాఠశాలను — మొత్తం గుండెను — కలిసి బ్రతికించగలదని గుర్తు చేసింది.
story.moral: Loud, exciting moments can make your heart beat fast. That feeling is normal—breathe, stay grounded, and keep going.
story.moral_te: బిగ్గర, ఉత్తేజకర క్షణాలు గుండెను త్వరగా కొట్టేలా చేయగలవు. అది సాధారణం — శ్వాస తీసుకోండి, నేలపై నిలబడండి, ముందుకు సాగండి.

1.activity: Next time a loud sound makes your heart race, place a hand on your chest and take four slow breaths before you move.
1.activity_te: తదుపరిసారి బిగ్గర ధ్వని గుండెను వేగవంతం చేసినప్పుడు, చేతిని ఛాతిపై ఉంచి నాలుగు నెమ్మది శ్వాసలు తీసుకుని తర్వాత కదలండి.

1.micro_theme: Ask a wise guide before a hard choice
1.micro_theme_te: కష్టమైన నిర్ణయం ముందు తెలివైన మార్గదర్శిని అడగండి

story.title: Ananya and the Two Clubs
story.content:
Ananya stared at the notice on her classroom board. Two clubs she loved had meetings on the same Saturday morning: Classical Dance Club and Science Explorers Club. Dance meant bharatanatyam steps she had practiced since age six. Science meant building a volcano model for the school fair.

She could not be in both places at once.

At lunch, her friends argued happily about their own choices. "Pick dance," said Kavya. "Pick science," said Rohan. Ananya ate her roti quietly. Her stomach felt twisted like a dupatta knot.

After school, she sat on the kitchen stool while Amma sliced mangoes. "I do not know what to choose," Ananya said. "Both feel important. If I pick wrong, I will disappoint someone—maybe even myself."

Amma wiped her hands and sat beside her. "Hard choices are not solved by shouting louder. They are solved by seeing clearly."

"But how?"

"Ask someone wise who knows you and will tell the truth gently."

Ananya thought of her grandfather, Thatha, who read the Gita every morning under the tulsi plant. She walked to the balcony where he was folding his reading glasses.

"Thatha," she said, "I have two paths and only two feet."

Thatha listened to every word without interrupting. When she finished, he nodded slowly. "In the Gita, before a very difficult day, Arjuna did not rush. He asked Krishna, his wise guide, to place the chariot where he could see clearly. He wanted help before moving forward."

"So asking is allowed?"

"Asking is brave," Thatha said. "A wise guide does not choose for you. A wise guide helps you see what matters in each path."

He asked three questions: Which club feeds the dream you carry longest? Which choice still lets you help your school? How will you feel tomorrow morning when you wake up?

Ananya answered honestly. Science fair was this month only. Dance was the language her body had spoken for years. She also remembered that her team needed one more presenter for the fair poster.

"I think I will do science this month," she said softly, "and ask my dance teacher if I can return after the fair."

Thatha smiled. "That sounds like a choice made with clear eyes, not fear."

The next Saturday, Ananya glued baking soda layers onto her volcano with steady hands. Her heart still missed dance music, but it did not feel lost. She had asked, listened, and chosen. The hard choice had become smaller because she had walked up to a wise guide first.
story.content_te:
అనన్య తరగతి బోర్డుపై నోటీసు చూస్తూ నిలబడింది. ఆమెకు ఇష్టమైన రెండు క్లబ్‌ల సమావేశాలు ఒకే శనివారం ఉదయం: క్లాసికల్ డ్యాన్స్ క్లబ్ మరియు సైన్స్ ఎక్స్‌ప్లోరర్స్ క్లబ్. నృత్యం అంటే ఆరేళ్ల నుంచి సాధన చేసిన భరతనాట్యం అడుగులు. సైన్స్ అంటే పాఠశాల మేళకు అగ్నిపర్వత మోడల్ నిర్మించడం.

ఆమె ఒకే సమయంలో రెండు చోట్ల ఉండలేరు.

భోజన సమయంలో స్నేహితులు తమ ఎంపికల గురించి సంతోషంగా వాదించారు. "నృత్యం ఎంచుకో," కావ్య అన్నది. "సైన్స్ ఎంచుకో," రోహన్ అన్నాడు. అనన్య నిశ్శబ్దంగా రొట్టి తిన్నది. కడుపు దుపట్టా ముడిలా చుట్టుకుంది.

పాఠశాల తర్వాత అమ్మ మామిడి కోస్తున్న సమయంలో అనన్య వంటగది స్టూల్‌పై కూర్చుంది. "ఏమి ఎంచుకోవాలో తెలియడం లేదు," అనన్య అన్నది. "రెండూ ముఖ్యమైనవి. తప్పు ఎంచుకుంటే ఎవరినో నిరాశ పరుస్తాను — బహుశా నన్ను కూడా."

అమ్మ చేతులు తుడిచి పక్కన కూర్చుంది. "కష్టమైన నిర్ణయాలు బిగ్గరగా అరుపులతో పరిష్కరించబడవు. స్పష్టంగా చూడడంతో పరిష్కరించబడతాయి."

"ఎలా?"

"మిమ్మల్ని తెలుసుకుని సత్యాన్ని మృదువుగా చెప్పే తెలివైన వ్యక్తిని అడగండి."

అనన్య తులసి చెట్టు కింద ప్రతి ఉదయం గీతా చదివే తాత గుర్తుకు వచ్చాడు. కళ్లద్దాలు మడుస్తున్న బాల్కనీ వద్దకు నడిచింది.

"తాత," ఆమె అన్నది, "రెండు దారులు ఉన్నాయి, రెండు పాదాలే ఉన్నాయి."

తాత ప్రతి మాట విన్నాడు, మధ్యలో అడగలేదు. ఆమె ముగించగానే నెమ్మదిగా తల వూనాడు. "గీతాలో చాలా కష్టమైన రోజు ముందు అర్జునుడు తొందరపెట్టలేదు. తన తెలివైన మార్గదర్శి కృష్ణుడిని రథాన్ని స్పష్టంగా చూడే చోట ఉంచమని అడిగాడు. ముందుకు వెళ్లే ముందు సహాయం కావాలని అడిగాడు."

"అడగడం సరైనదా?"

"అడగడం ధైర్యం," తాత అన్నారు. "తెలివైన మార్గదర్శి మీ కోసం ఎంపిక చేయడు. ప్రతి దారిలో ఏమి ముఖ్యమో చూడడంలో సహాయం చేస్తాడు."

తాత మూడు ప్రశ్నలు అడిగాడు: ఏ క్లబ్ మీరు ఎక్కువ కాలం పోషించిన కలను పోషిస్తుంది? ఏ ఎంపిక మీ పాఠశాలకు ఇంకా సహాయం చేస్తుంది? రేపు ఉదయం మేల్కొన్నప్పుడు మీరు ఎలా అనిపిస్తారు?

అనన్య నిజాయితీగా సమాధానం చెప్పింది. సైన్స్ మేళ ఈ నెల మాత్రమే. నృత్యం సంవత్సరాలుగా ఆమె శరీరం మాట్లాడే భాష. మేళ పోస్టర్‌కు మరో ప్రదర్శకురాలు కావాలని గుర్తుంది.

"ఈ నెల సైన్స్ చేస్తాను," ఆమె మృదువుగా అన్నది, "మేళ తర్వాత నృత్య ఉపాధ్యాయిని తిరిగి రావచ్చా అని అడుగుతాను."

తాత నవ్వాడు. "భయంతో కాదు, స్పష్టమైన కళ్లతో చేసిన ఎంపిక లాగా ఉంది."

తదుపరి శనివారం అనన్య తన అగ్నిపర్వతానికి బేకింగ్ సోడా పొరలు స్థిరమైన చేతులతో అతికించింది. గుండె ఇంకా నృత్య సంగీతం మిస్ అవుతోంది, కానీ కోల్పోయినట్లు అనిపించలేదు. ఆమె అడిగింది, విన్నది, ఎంచుకుంది. తెలివైన మార్గదర్శిని ముందుగా సంప్రదించినందువల్ల కష్టమైన నిర్ణయం చిన్నదిగా మారింది.
story.moral: Before a hard choice, ask a wise grown-up who knows you. Good guidance helps you see clearly—it does not decide for you.
story.moral_te: కష్టమైన నిర్ణయం ముందు మిమ్మల్ని తెలిసిన తెలివైన పెద్దవారిని అడగండి. మంచి మార్గదర్శనం స్పష్టంగా చూడడంలో సహాయం చేస్తుంది — మీ కోసం నిర్ణయించదు.

1.activity: Think of one hard choice you have now. Ask a trusted grown-up one clear question before you decide.
1.activity_te: మీకు ఇప్పుడు ఉన్న ఒక కష్టమైన నిర్ణయం గుర్తు చేసుకుని, నిర్ణయించే ముందు నమ్మకమైన పెద్దవారిని ఒక స్పష్టమైన ప్రశ్న అడగండి.

1.title: Stop and Look

story.title: Rishi and the Wet Rangoli
story.content:
Sports Day at Lotus School was always exciting. This year, Rishi's class had made a huge rangoli of a sun and lotus at the entrance to the running track. They had worked since dawn with coloured rice flour, and the design still glistened with wet chalk lines.

Rishi was chosen for the relay race—the last runner, the fastest legs in Class 4. His team counted on him.

When the whistle blew for the first heat, Rishi's body buzzed like a live wire. He watched his teammate round the bend and slap the baton into his palm. Now it was his turn. His feet wanted to fly.

He shot forward—then skidded. His shoe grazed the edge of the rangoli. Red and yellow powder smeared into a messy streak. A younger girl gasped. Rishi's face burned with shame.

"Rishi!" called Coach Meena from the side. She did not shout angrily. She clapped once, sharp and clear. "Come here."

Rishi walked over, eyes on the ground.

"You love speed," Coach Meena said. "Speed is good. But where did your eyes go?"

"I only thought about the baton," Rishi mumbled.

"Before you act, look. Left, right, ground, people."

That evening, Rishi told his father what had happened while they watered the terrace tulsi pots.

Appa set down the steel mug. "In the Gita, Krishna moved Arjuna's chariot to the middle of the field so he could look carefully at everyone before choosing his next step. Even in a great hurry, wise people pause to see the whole picture."

Rishi pictured the smeared lotus. "I did not pause."

"Tomorrow, try again with your eyes open."

The next heat was louder. Parents cheered. Drums tapped in the distance. Rishi crouched at the line, baton ready, heart pounding—but this time he made a small plan. When the baton touched his hand, he would count: one look at the track, one look at the rangoli border, one look at the finish line.

The slap came. Rishi breathed. One—clear track ahead. Two—rangoli safe on his left. Three—Dev waiting at the line.

Then he ran.

His feet pounded the dry ground. He did not cut the corner too tight. He did not bump the boy from the next lane. He crossed the finish line breathless and grinning.

Coach Meena gave him a thumbs up. "Same speed. Better eyes."

Rishi looked back at the rangoli, still bright and whole. He had learned that a second of looking could protect a morning of work—and keep his run fair and strong.

లోటస్ పాఠశాలలో స్పోర్ట్స్ డే ఎప్పుడూ ఉత్తేజకరం. ఈ సంవత్సరం రిషి తరగతి పరుగు మార్గం ప్రవేశద్వారం వద్ద సూర్యుడు, తామర పెద్ద రంగోలి వేసింది. ఉదయం నుంచి రంగు బియ్యం పిండితో పని చేసి, డిజైన్ ఇంకా తడి చాక్ గీతలతో మెరుస్తోంది.

రిషి రిలే పరుగుకు ఎంపికయ్యాడు — చివరి రన్నర్, నాల్గవ తరగతిలో అతి వేగమైన కాళ్లు. జట్టు అతనిపై ఆధారపడింది.

మొదటి హీట్ విజిల్ ఊదగానే రిషి శరీరం తాజా తీగలా ఝనిలాడింది. తన టీమ్‌మేట్ మోడు తిప్పి బ్యాటన్ అతని అరచేతిలో కొట్టడం చూశాడు. ఇప్పుడు అతని వంతు. పాదాలు ఎగిరిపోవాలనుకున్నాయి.

అతను ముందుకు దూసుకుపోయాడు — అప్పుడు జారిపోయాడు. బూటు రంగోలి అంచును తాకింది. ఎరుపు, పసుపు పొడి అస్తవ్యస్త పట్టుగా మాశ్ అయింది. ఒక చిన్న అమ్మాయి ఊపిరి ఆగిపోయింది. రిషి ముఖం సిగ్గుతో మండింది.

"రిషి!" పక్కన నుంచి కోచ్ మీనా పిలిచారు. కోపంగా అరవలేదు. ఒకసారి స్పష్టంగా చప్పటు కొట్టారు. "ఇక్కడికి రా."

రిషి నేల చూస్తూ నడిచాడు.

"నీకు వేగం ఇష్టం," కోచ్ మీనా అన్నారు. "వేగం మంచిది. కానీ నీ కళ్లు ఎక్కడికి వెళ్లాయి?"

"బ్యాటన్ గురించే ఆలోచించాను," రిషి గుసగుసలాడాడు.

"చర్య చేయే ముందు చూడు. ఎడమ, కుడి, నేల, ప్రజలు."

ఆ సాయంత్రం రిషి తావేడిపై తులసి కుండీలకు నీరు పోస్తూ తండ్రికి జరిగినది చెప్పాడు.

అప్పా స్టీల్ మగ్ కింద ఉంచాడు. "గీతాలో కృష్ణుడు అర్జునుడి రథాన్ని మైదానం మధ్యలోకి తీసుకువెళ్లాడు, తదుపరి అడుగు ఎక్కడ వేయాలో నిర్ణయించే ముందు అందరినీ జాగ్రత్తగా చూడేలా. గొప్ప తొందరలో కూడా తెలివైన వారు మొత్తం చిత్రాన్ని చూడడానికి క్షణం ఆగుతారు."

రిషి మాశ్ అయిన తామరను ఊహించాడు. "నేను ఆగలేదు."

"రేపు కళ్లు తెరిచి మళ్లీ ప్రయత్నించు."

తదుపరి హీట్ ఇంకా బిగ్గరగా ఉంది. తల్లిదండ్రులు ప్రోత్సహించారు. దూరంగా డ్రమ్స్ కొట్టాయి. రిషి లైన్ వద్ద కుంగి బ్యాటన్ సిద్ధంగా, గుండె బిగ్గరగా — కానీ ఈసారి చిన్న ప్లాన్ చేశాడు. బ్యాటన్ చేతికి తగిలినప్పుడు లెక్కిస్తాను: ఒకసారి మార్గం, ఒకసారి రంగోలి అంచు, ఒకసారి ఫినిష్ లైన్.

బ్యాటన్ వచ్చింది. రిషి శ్వాస తీసుకున్నాడు. ఒకటి — ముందు మార్గం స్పష్టం. రెండు — ఎడమవైపు రంగోలి సురక్షితం. మూడు — ఫినిష్ లైన్ వద్ద దేవ్ వేచి ఉన్నాడు.

అప్పుడు పరిగెత్తాడు.

పాదాలు ఎండిన నేలపై మోగాయి. మోడు చాలా బిగ్గరగా తిప్పలేదు. పక్క లేన్ అబ్బాయిని ఢీకొనలేదు. శ్వాస ఆగిపోయి నవ్వుతూ ఫినిష్ లైన్ దాటాడు.

కోచ్ మీనా థమ్స్ అప్ ఇచ్చారు. "అదే వేగం. మంచి కళ్లు."

రిషి వెనుకకు రంగోలి చూశాడు — ఇంకా తేజోమయంగా, పూర్తిగా ఉంది. ఒక క్షణం చూడడం ఉదయం పాటు పనిని కాపాడగలదని, తన పరుగును న్యాయంగా, బలంగా ఉంచగలదని నేర్చుకున్నాడు.
story.moral: Before you rush forward, pause and look around. A careful glance can protect your work and your path.

story.title: Ananya Backstage at Annual Day
story.content:
Ananya had practiced her little deer dance twenty times in the corner of her bedroom. Amma clapped each time. Appa filmed on his phone. Her small antler headband sat on the study table like a crown waiting for Saturday.

Saturday was school Annual Day.

In the morning, Amma plaited Ananya's hair with fresh white mogras. "You know every step," Amma said, tying the last flower. "Your feet have already danced this in your sleep."

Ananya smiled. But when the school bus dropped her at the back gate of the auditorium, something strange happened. Her stomach fluttered like the pigeons above the water tank. Her palms turned damp. The sitar music from inside sounded like a giant heartbeat.

Backstage, cotton clouds hung from ropes. Teachers rushed with safety pins. Ananya peered through the curtain slit and saw rows of parents—Amma in her blue saree, Appa craning his neck, Nanamma waving a folded fan.

Ananya's knees felt loose, like cooked rice that would not hold shape. Worse still, when she tried to remember the first step of her dance in her head, the words simply vanished. Step left, bend low, hop twice—where did that go?

"Amma says I know it," she whispered to herself, but her voice sounded thin.

Miss Priya, her dance teacher, knelt beside her. "What are you feeling, Ananya?"

"My legs are wobbly. And my brain forgot the dance."

Miss Priya nodded as if this were perfectly ordinary news. "In the old Gita story, great warrior Arjuna stood before a huge battle. He was brave and well trained. Still, his body shook and his mouth went dry. His mind went blank too. Fear touched his legs and his thoughts at the same time."

Ananya stared. "Even warriors?"

"Even warriors. Fear is not only a thought in your head. It is also cold hands and wobbly knees. They can come together."

Miss Priya held out her palms. "Feel your feet on the floor. Name three things: your antlers, your music, your Amma's smile in row three."

Ananya pressed her toes down. Antlers. Sitar count. Amma's face.

The curtain opened.

Ananya walked to the centre. Her knees still wobbled a little, but her feet remembered. Left, bend, hop, hop—just as she had practised on the cool bedroom tiles. When she finished, the auditorium clapped like monsoon rain on a tin roof.

Afterward, Ananya told Appa, "My body was scared and my mind forgot—but my feet did not."

అనన్య తన చిన్న జింక నృత్యాన్ని బెడ్‌రూమ్ మూలలో ఇరవై సార్లు సాధన చేసింది. అమ్మ ప్రతిసారీ చప్పట్లు కొట్టింది. అప్పా ఫోన్‌లో వీడియో తీశాడు. చిన్న కొమ్ముల తలపాగ చదువు మేజా మీద శనివారం కోసం ఎదురు చూస్తున్న కిరీటంలా పడుకుంది.

ఆ శనివారం పాఠశాల వార్షిక ఉత్సవం.

ఉదయం అమ్మ అనన్య జుట్టులో తాజా తెల్లని మొగ్రాలు చుట్టింది. "నీకు ప్రతి అడుగు తెలుసు," చివరి పువ్వు కట్టుతూ అమ్మ అన్నది. "నీ పాదాలు నిద్రలోనే ఇది నృత్యం చేశాయి."

అనన్య నవ్వింది. కానీ పాఠశాల బస్సు ఆడిటోరియం వెనుక గేట్‌కు దించినప్పుడు ఏదో వింత జరిగింది. నీటి ట్యాంక్ పైన ఉన్న పigeonsల처럼 కడుపులో flutter. అరచేతులు తడిగా మారాయి. లోపల సితార్ సంగీతం ఒ huge heartbeatలా వినిపించింది.

Backstage, cotton clouds ropesకు వేలాడాయి. Teachers safety pinsతో hurry. అనన్య curtain slit ద్వara parents rows చూసింది — blue sareeలో అమ్మ, neck stretch చేస్తున్న అప్పా, folded fan wave చేస్తున్న నానమ్మ.

అనన్య knees loose — cooked rice shape hold చేయలేనట్లు. worse still, first step mindలో remember చేయడానికి try చేసినప్పుడు words vanished. Step left, bend low, hop twice — అది ఎక్కడ?

"అమ్మ నాకు తెలుసు అని చెప్పింది," గుసగుసలాడింది, voice thin.

Miss Priya dance teacher knelt beside. "ఏమి feel అవుతోంది, అనన్య?"

"Legs wobbly. Brain dance మర్చిపోయింది."

Miss Priya nodded ordinary newsలaga. "పాత Gita storyలో great warrior Arjuna huge battle ముందు stood. Brave, well trained. Still body shook, mouth dry. Mind blank. Fear legs and thoughts same time touch."

"Warriors kuda?"

"Warriors kuda. Fear head thought మాత్రమే కాదు. Cold hands, wobbly knees kuda. Together raavachu."

Miss Priya palms held out. "Feet floor feel. Three things name: antlers, music, row three lo Amma smile."

Ananya toes pressed. Antlers. Sitar count. Amma face.

Curtain opened.

Ananya centre walked. Knees still wobbly, feet remembered. Left, bend, hop, hop — bedroom tiles practice. Finished — auditorium clapped monsoon rain tin roof.

Afterward Appa told: "Body scared, mind forgot — feet did not."
story.moral: Fear can make your legs wobble and your mind go blank at the same time. Slow breaths and one small step can still carry you forward.

1.title: The Spinning Choice

story.title: Mia and the Project Table
story.content:
Mia's group had to pick one poster topic by Friday: rivers, space, or animals.

All three sounded exciting on Monday. By Wednesday, none of them did.

At the project table in the library corner, chart paper lay blank while her teammates argued. Dev wanted space rockets because they looked cool on posters. Leela wanted rivers because her grandmother told stories about the Godavari. Rohan wanted animals because he had a book of tiger pictures at home.

Mia sat in the middle, pencil hovering, mind spinning. Every choice felt wrong. If she picked space, Leela would look sad. If she picked rivers, Dev would groan. If she picked animals, Rohan would grin — but Mia secretly loved stars more than tigers.

Her head hurt the way it does when you turn in circles too fast.

That evening, Mia told Amma she could not decide anything. Amma was folding clothes on the bed and did not rush to fix it.

"In the old Gita story," Amma said, "brave Arjuna stood before a huge day and saw problems everywhere. His mind went round and round. Confusion is not because you are silly. It is because you care about more than one good thing."

"But we need one topic," Mia whispered.

"Yes. So shrink the storm. Ask one small question: what do you want to learn most for yourself?"

Mia thought. Stars were beautiful, but she had already done a space chart in Class 3. Tigers were handsome, but Rohan's book would do most of the work. Rivers — she remembered sitting with Nani on the bank near Rajahmundry, throwing pebbles and watching light dance on water.

"Rivers," she said suddenly. "Because I want to draw the journey from mountain to sea."

The next day at school, Mia told her group her reason — not who would be upset least, but what she truly wanted to learn. Dev agreed when she promised a small rocket drawing in the corner for space-lovers. Rohan offered his tiger book for the border animals. Leela smiled so wide Mia felt warm in her chest.

One honest question had stopped the spinning.
story.content_te:
మియా గ్రూప్ శుక్రవారం కి ఒక పోస్టర్ టాపిక్ ఎంచుకోవాలి: నదులు, అంతరిక్షం, లేదా జంతువులు.

మూడు సోమవారం ఉత్తేజకరంగా వినిపించాయి. బుధవారం కి ఏదీ కాదు.

లైబ్రరీ మూల ప్రాజెక్ట్ టేబుల్‌పై చార్ట్ పేపర్ ఖాళీ — teammates వాదిస్తున్నారు. దేవ్ స్పేస్ రాకెట్లు — పోస్టర్‌లో cool. లీలా నదులు — అమ్మమ్మ గోదావరి కథలు. రోహన్ జంతువులు — ఇంట్లో పులి చిత్రాల పుస్తకం.

మియా మధ్య, pencil hover, mind spinning. ప్రతి choice wrong. space — లీలా sad. rivers — దేవ్ groan. animals — రోహన్ grin, కానీ మియా stars tigers కంటే ఇష్టం.

తల circles too fast లా నొప్పి.

సాయంత్రం అమ్మ decide చేయలేకపోతున్నాను చెప్పింది. అమ్మ బెడ్‌పై బట్టలు fold — hurry fix చేయలేదు.

"పాత Gita story," అమ్మ, "brave Arjuna huge day ముందు stood, problems everywhere. mind round round. confusion silly కాదు — one కంటే ఎక్కువ good things care."

"one topic kavali," మియా whisper.

"Shrink storm. one small question: nuvvu learn చేయాలనుకున్నది ఏమిటి?"

మియా thought. stars beautiful, Class 3 lo space chart already. tigers handsome, రోహన్ book work చేస్తుంది. rivers — Rajahmundry bank Nani తో pebbles, water light dance.

"Rivers," suddenly. "mountain to sea journey draw చేయాలి."

next day school reason చెప్పింది — least upset కాదు, truly learn. దేవ్ corner lo small rocket promise — agree. రోహన్ border animals book. లీలా wide smile — chest warm.

1.title: People Before Prizes
1.micro_theme: Winning is not more important than people

story.title: Tina and the Spelling Bee
story.content:
Tina and Leela had studied together every Thursday after school for two months.

They quizzed each other on hard words — rhythm, conscience, bouquet — while Tina's Amma brought sliced mango and Leela's Appa timed them with his old stopwatch. They were best friends, and both had reached the Class 5 spelling bee final.

On stage, the auditorium felt enormous. The microphone looked like a silver flower. Tina knew the final word before she spoke it: maintenance. She had missed it once in practice and Leela had helped her remember the "ten" in the middle.

She spelled it correctly. The audience clapped. Tina won the small trophy with the school emblem — gold, shiny, heavier than she expected.

Leela hugged her backstage, but Tina saw the quick blink that meant her friend was hiding disappointment. That night, Tina could not enjoy the trophy on her shelf. She kept thinking of Leela walking home without the ribbon.

At dinner, Thatha noticed her quiet face. He told her about Arjuna in the Gita — how he looked across a field and saw people he loved, and said winning kingdoms and prizes was not worth hurting them. Tina did not have a kingdom. She had a trophy and a best friend.

The next morning, Tina brought the trophy to school and placed it on the desk between them. "This belongs to both of us," she said. "You taught me maintenance."

Leela's eyes shone. "You earned it."

"I earned the spelling," Tina said. "We earned the studying."

They made a pact: next year, they would quiz each other again — whoever wins, the other gets the first hug, not the first jealous thought.

Tina still liked winning. But the trophy on her shelf looked brighter when it meant friendship, not just first place.

1.title: When Love Feels Heavy
1.micro_theme: Love for family can make duty feel painful

story.title: Kabir and the House Captain Vote
story.content:
Kabir's older brother Arjun was the star of Blue House — fastest runner, loudest cheers, everyone's favourite.

When house captain elections came, half the class wrote Arjun's name before the bell rang. Kabir was proud. He also wanted to try. He had organized the recycling drive. He had helped younger students read during lunch. His name felt small next to his brother's.

On voting day, Kabir stared at the slip on his desk. His chest felt tight, like a knot he could not undo. If he voted for himself, would Arjun think he was disloyal? If he voted for Arjun, would he betray his own work?

At home, Kabir sat on the kitchen step while Amma rolled chapatis. "My heart hurts both ways," he said.

Amma listened. "In the Gita, Arjuna loved his cousins and teachers so much that doing his duty felt like breaking his own heart. Love and duty can pull in opposite directions. That pain is real."

"So what do I do?"

"You tell the truth gently. Vote for the person you believe will serve the house — including yourself if that is honest. Then speak to your brother with love."

Kabir voted for himself. His hand shook a little, but the knot loosened.

Arjun won by three votes anyway. Kabir walked to him after the results.

"I voted for me," he said. "Not because I love you less. Because I tried too."

Arjun ruffled his hair — hard, brotherly. "Good. Next year, run again."

Duty had felt painful because love was real. Honest words made both lighter.

1.title: One Piece Before Quitting
1.micro_theme: Giving up begins in the mind

story.title: Neha and the Thousand Pieces
story.content:
Neha opened the thousand-piece puzzle box and immediately wanted to close it again.

The picture on the cover showed a bright blue peacock spread across a garden. It looked beautiful and impossible. She poured the pieces onto the living room mat — a noisy avalanche of cardboard. Within five minutes, her mind whispered: You cannot do this. You are too small for this. Put it away.

Neha slumped forward, chin on her knees. Her older brother Kiran walked past, paused, and sat down without teasing her.

"Too big?" he asked.

"My brain already quit," Neha said.

Kiran smiled. "In the Gita story, great warrior Arjuna sat down and wanted to stop before the hard day even began. Giving up started in his mind first — his body was still strong."

"So he was lazy?"

"No. He was overwhelmed. Big tasks scare minds before hands."

Kiran flipped one piece right-side up. It was a plain blue edge — boring, simple. "Just one piece today. Not the peacock. Not the thousand. One."

Neha exhaled. She clicked one edge piece into another. Then two more found each other — both sky blue. By bedtime she had a tiny corner of the border. It was almost nothing on the mat. But her mind had not quit.

The next day she added five pieces after homework. Then ten on Sunday with Appa's help finding colours. Week by week, the peacock's eye appeared, then the neck, then the tail.

When the last piece snapped in place a month later, Neha did not mainly feel proud of the picture. She felt proud that the first voice — I cannot — had not been the last voice.

Giving up had begun in her mind. One small piece had begun the answer.

2.title: Stand Up Again

story.title: Meera and the Dance Stage
story.content:
Meera had practiced her school dance for three whole weeks. She knew every step — tap, spin, bow. She counted beats in the shower and in the lunch line. On the day of the show, the hall was full. Parents sat in rows like a garden of bright shirts and eager faces. The stage lights were warm on her cheeks. Meera's heart beat fast, but she smiled. This was her moment.

Then, halfway through the spin, her foot slipped on a shiny patch of floor someone had polished too much. Down she went — knees first, then hands. The music kept playing for three more beats that felt like three hours. For one terrible second, the whole room seemed to hold its breath.

Meera's eyes filled with hot tears. She wanted to crawl behind the curtain and never come out. "I'm done," she whispered to the floor. "I'm the girl who fell."

After the show, her Amma knelt beside her in the hallway where the smell of jasmine garlands hung in the air. She did not say, "Don't cry." She said, "That fall hurt — your knees and your pride. Both matter."

Coach Priya joined them with a water bottle and a clean towel. "Even the best dancers fall," she said. "On the biggest stages in the world, people fall. Courage is not never falling. Courage is standing up again."

Meera remembered something Amma had read from the Gita at bedtime. When Arjuna felt weak with sorrow, Krishna did not tell him to stay on the ground forever. Krishna told him to rise — to stand up for what mattered, even when his heart felt heavy.

The next morning, Meera's knees were bruised purple, but she put on her dance shoes anyway. She went to the empty hall and stood in the middle of the stage where the shiny patch still gleamed. She took a breath. She did one slow spin. Then another. Her foot stayed steady.

"Again," she told herself quietly.

At practice that week, she fell once more — a small wobble, not a crash. This time she laughed, stood up, and bowed to her reflection in the mirror as if the whole audience were cheering not for a perfect girl, but for a brave one who got back up.

Falling had been part of her story. Standing up again was the part she chose.

story.title: Rohan and the Report Card
story.content:
Rohan opened his report card on the kitchen table and felt his stomach drop like an elevator. Maths — a red mark he did not expect. Science — lower than last term. He had studied at the dining table every evening. He really had. But the numbers on the paper looked like a door closing in his face.

He ran to his room and buried his face in his pillow, which smelled like his laundry soap and disappointment. "I'm stupid," he muffled into the fabric. "I'll never be good enough."

His Chithi — his aunt — knocked softly and sat on the edge of his bed. She did not grab the report card right away. She waited until Rohan's shoulders stopped shaking, her hand resting on the blanket.

"Tell me the sad part," she said.

"I worked hard and still failed," Rohan whispered. "Everyone will think I'm dumb."

Chithi nodded. "That hurts. It is okay to feel sad today. Sadness is not the enemy. Staying stuck in it forever is the trap."

Then she opened a small book on her phone — a picture of Krishna and Arjuna on a chariot between two armies. "When Arjuna's heart was breaking on the battlefield, Krishna did not start with hard rules. His first teaching was gentle but firm. He said: the wise do not grieve for what cannot be changed. What has happened has happened. Crying forever will not turn yesterday's mark into today's A-plus."

Rohan peeked at her. "So I shouldn't care?"

"No, dear heart. Care very much. Care enough to learn. But do not drown in a sadness that keeps you from tomorrow's work. Grieve the mark — then rise."

They walked back to the kitchen together. Chithi made hot chocolate with extra foam. Rohan spread his books on the table. One maths problem at a time, they found where he had gone wrong — not because he was stupid, but because one tricky step about fractions had confused him every time.

By bedtime, Rohan still felt disappointed. The red mark was still real. But the heavy blanket of "never good enough" had lifted a little. He wrote on a sticky note and stuck it on his desk: Ask Chithi for maths help every Tuesday.

Sadness had visited. Wisdom had not asked him to pretend he was happy. It had asked him not to stay fallen inside his mind.

story.title: Ananya and the Courtyard Tree
story.content:
In the middle of Ananya's courtyard stood an old neem tree with rough bark that scratched her palms when she climbed. She had grown up running around its trunk, tying friendship bracelets on a low branch, and sharing ice pops in its shade with the neighbor kids.

In summer, its shade was cool and green. In monsoon, rain drummed on the broad leaves like fingers on a table. In winter, the tree looked sleepy and bare, honest about resting. In spring, tiny new leaves appeared like green fireworks against the blue sky.

One year, Ananya's family moved to a new city for her Appa's work. The new flat had no courtyard and no neem tree — only a balcony the size of a rug. Ananya's room felt too small. She missed her old friends, her old street with the corner shop that always gave extra chutney, and the tree that had watched her grow taller every year.

"Nothing here is the same," she told her Paati, her grandmother, on a video call, tears sliding down her cheeks. "I want to go back."

Paati smiled gently on the screen, her silver earrings catching the light. "Come to the courtyard when you visit next month. Bring your drawing book and your patience."

When Ananya returned for holidays, Paati was waiting under the neem tree with two cups of warm milk and a plate of murukku. "Look up," Paati said.

Ananya looked. Some branches were thinner than she remembered. New shoots had grown where old ones had broken in a storm last year. Birds had built a fresh nest, busy with chirps.

"The tree changed," Ananya said slowly.

"Yes. And it is still the same tree. Krishna teaches that bodies and days change like seasons — childhood to growing up, summer to winter. What feels happy today may feel hard tomorrow, and hard things soften again. The wise know: change is the way life breathes."

Paati opened Ananya's old drawing book. Page after page showed the same tree in four seasons — green, gold, grey, bright green again.

Ananya added a new page: the tree in a windstorm, and then calm after. She drew herself beside it in her new school uniform, smaller in the corner but still there, still smiling a little.

Back in the city, she pinned the drawing above her desk. When lonely days came, she touched the paper and remembered: seasons turn. Feelings turn. She was not stuck in one winter forever.

2.title: The Broken Toy

story.title: Kabir and the Wooden Elephant
story.content:
Kabir's wooden elephant was his favorite toy in the whole world. Appa had carved it from a smooth piece of teak on a rainy weekend, with tiny ears and a trunk that curled just right. Kabir took it everywhere — to breakfast, to the park, even toward the bathroom door until Amma said absolutely not.

One rainy afternoon, Kabir's cousin Leela came to visit with her toy car. They built a fort from pillows and raced their toys across the carpet like a tiny highway. Leela's car bumped hard into the elephant on a sharp turn. Crack. The trunk broke clean off and rolled under the sofa with a small wooden clack.

Kabir stared at the broken toy in his hands. His chest felt like someone had squeezed it tight. "You broke it!" he shouted. Leela's eyes went wide and shiny. She whispered, "Sorry," but Kabir would not look at her. He grabbed the elephant's body and ran to his room, slamming the door harder than he meant.

That evening, Ajji — his grandmother — found him sitting on the floor with glue, tissue, and tears. "It won't be the same," Kabir said. "Nothing good stays."

Ajji sat beside him, slow and steady as the rain on the window. "The trunk broke. That is true. Your sadness is true too. Do not pretend you are not hurt."

She picked up the trunk and the body carefully. "And this is also true: you are still Kabir. Leela is still sorry. Appa's love is still in every carved line on the body. Pleasure and pain visit every person, like sun and rain on the same roof. The wise do not let one broken afternoon steal all truth."

They glued the trunk together with sticky fingers. It was not perfect — a thin line showed where the break had been. Ajji said, "See that line? It tells a story. The elephant fell and was mended with love."

The next day, Kabir showed Leela the mended elephant at breakfast. "You can still play," he said quietly. "Just — careful near the trunk."

Leela nodded so hard her curls bounced. They built a slower, gentler fort.

Kabir learned that day: toys break, days hurt, but the deeper truths — love, kindness, who you are — can stay steady through the storm.

2.title: The Little Lamp

story.title: Diya and Mango the Goldfish
story.content:
Diya was six years old, and her best friend in the whole world was a goldfish named Mango. Every morning before school, Diya tapped the glass bowl and whispered, "Good morning, Mango!" Mango would swim in happy circles, his orange tail flashing like a tiny flame in the water.

Diya's Thatha lived in the yellow house next door. He had a small brass diya that he lit every evening in his garden, among the marigolds that smelled sweet and bright. "The flame is small," Thatha would say, "but it is brave. It shines steady even when the wind whispers."

One Tuesday, Diya ran to the fish bowl after breakfast and stopped. Mango was not swimming. He lay very still at the bottom, like a leaf resting on quiet water. Diya's chest felt heavy. Tears rolled down her cheeks before she even knew she was crying.

"Is Mango gone forever?" she asked her Amma, her voice very small.

Amma held Diya close and did not hurry the tears. "Your love for Mango is real," Amma said softly. "It is okay to feel very sad."

That evening, Thatha found Diya sitting on his garden step, staring at the marigolds without seeing them. He sat beside her without speaking at first. Then he brought out the brass diya and lit it with a match. The flame popped alive — small, golden, steady.

"Do you see how the flame dances?" Thatha asked gently.

Diya nodded, sniffling.

"Some people think the soul — the real aliveness inside Mango, inside you, inside me — can be squashed or blown out, like a candle in a big wind. But Krishna teaches Arjuna something wise. The one who thinks the soul can be killed, or that the soul kills — neither knows the truth. The soul is never born, and it never dies."

Diya looked at the flame. "But Mango's body stopped."

"Yes, little one. Bodies start and stop, like waves on a pond. Mango's body was like the diya's wax — it held his light for a while. But the light itself?" Thatha smiled. "The light keeps going."

"Where is Mango now?"

Thatha pointed to the flame, then to Diya's heart. "Where does the flame go when we snuff the wick? It joins the great light. Mango's swimming made you happy. Your happy memories are still here." He placed his warm palm on Diya's chest. "That love did not die. It lives inside you — a light that never goes out."

A butterfly with orange wings floated over the marigolds and landed on the fence, opening and closing its wings like Mango's old tail.

Diya whispered, "Thank you, Mango, for the circles."

That night, Diya drew Mango with a glowing heart and placed the picture beside her bed. She still missed him. Grief did not vanish like magic. But the fear that Mango was completely erased began to soften, like morning light filling a dark room.

Before sleep, Diya looked at the little lamp Thatha had given her — a tiny brass diya on her windowsill. Amma helped her light it. The flame was small and brave. The soul, like the flame, never truly goes out.

story.title: Isha and the Old Uniform
story.content:
Isha was cleaning the storeroom with Thatha on a dusty Saturday when she found a small trunk in the corner behind old saree bundles. Inside were clothes from long ago — a tiny frock with yellow flowers, soft booties, and a school uniform two sizes too small with a name tag sewn inside.

"Is that you?" Isha asked, holding up the little uniform against her chest.

Thatha laughed, his eyes crinkling like paper folds. "That was me at your age. Same boy. Smaller clothes."

Isha tried the uniform over her shorts, giggling at the mirror. The sleeves stopped at her elbows. "I look silly," she said.

"You look like a growing girl wearing an old shell," Thatha said. He sat on an old chair and pulled at his current white kurta. "This body is like a set of clothes. When I was small, I wore small clothes. Now I wear these. One day, this body will grow old and tired, like a shirt worn thin at the elbows. But the wearer — the real me inside — keeps going, like you keep being you even when your school uniform changes every year."

Isha thought about that, tracing the name tag with her finger. Last year she had been in class one. Now class two. New shoes. A new height mark on the kitchen wall. "So my body changes like outfits?"

"Exactly," Thatha said. "Krishna tells Arjuna: just as a person throws away worn clothes and puts on new ones, the soul wears new bodies. Fire cannot burn the soul. Water cannot drown it. Weapons cannot cut it. The real you is unhurtable — deep inside."

Isha touched her own arm, then her heart. "So when I scrape my knee, it's the clothes — not the real me?"

"The scrape hurts," Thatha said kindly. "Bodies matter. We care for them. But when you feel afraid that one bump means you are broken forever — remember the wearer is whole."

They folded the old uniform gently and placed it back in the trunk like a treasure. Isha drew two figures in her notebook — small Isha in the tiny uniform, tall Isha in today's blue dress — with the same bright star drawn on both chests.

"Same star," she told Thatha.

"Same you," he answered, closing the trunk with a soft click.

2.title: Win or Lose, Steady Heart
2.micro_theme: Do your part with a calm heart

story.title: Arjun at Sports Day
story.content:
Sports day was the loudest day of the year at Arjun's school. Banners flapped in the wind. Drums beat. Parents cheered from the stands like a roaring river that never paused.

Arjun was running in the hundred-metre race. He had trained every morning for two weeks — stretching on the porch, sprinting to the corner tree, drinking water, sleeping early when Amma insisted. His legs felt strong. His mind felt ready, like a coiled spring.

At the starting line, white chalk sharp against the red track, his friend Dev whispered, "If you don't win, everyone will forget you by lunch."

Arjun's stomach tightened into a knot. For a moment, winning felt like the only thing that mattered — more than the run itself, more than the months of practice.

Then Coach Meera clapped her hands once, sharp and clear. "Run your race. Not someone else's. Do your best with a steady heart — win or lose, you are still Arjun."

The whistle blew. Arjun ran. Wind rushed past his ears. His feet found the track. Arms pumped. One runner pulled ahead on the last stretch — a blur in the next lane. Arjun crossed the line second, not first.

His first feeling was a punch of disappointment so heavy he wanted to kick the grass and hide behind the equipment shed. Dev looked away, awkward, as if second place were catching.

Coach Meera brought two cups of water. "How was your effort?" she asked, looking at his face, not the scoreboard.

"I tried everything," Arjun said, breath slowing.

"Then hold your head up. Krishna tells Arjuna on the battlefield: you have a right to action, not to the fruits. Treat victory and defeat the same — both are clouds passing. What stays is the courage to run fully."

Arjun watched the winner receive a ribbon. He clapped. His clap was real, not fake. He felt something steady inside — not happy about losing, but not broken either.

Later, he helped pick up cones and cheered until his voice went hoarse for the relay team. Amma hugged him at the gate, smelling like sunscreen and pride. "I saw you run with your whole heart," she said.

That night, Arjun pinned his race number on the wall — not because he won, but because he had shown up and run true. Win or lose, his heart had stayed on its feet.

2.title: The Practice Room
2.micro_theme: Focus on effort instead of rewards

story.title: Sia and the Music Exam
story.content:
Sia loved the shiny medals on her sister's shelf. Gold, silver, bronze — they caught the morning light like small suns lined up in a row. Sia wanted one more than anything. She imagined the weight of it on her neck after the music exam.

When her music teacher announced an exam with a special certificate for distinction, Sia's eyes lit up. "If I get distinction, Appa will buy me a medal," she told her mirror, adjusting her ponytail.

For the first week, she practiced her piano piece — but only the hard parts that sounded impressive when someone walked past the living room. She skipped the slow beginning because nobody clapped for that. She rushed the ending because finishing fast felt like winning.

Her teacher, Mr. Daniel, listened with his head tilted and shook it gently. "You are playing for the medal, not for the music."

Sia frowned, fingers stiff on the keys. "What's wrong with wanting a medal?"

"Nothing," Mr. Daniel said. "But Krishna gives a famous teaching: you have a right to your work, not to the reward. When you cling only to the prize, fear steals your joy. When you love the effort, your hands grow honest."

Sia did not understand fully, but she tried. She began waking ten minutes early to play the whole piece from the first quiet note — even the parts nobody noticed. She counted beats slowly. She fixed one sticky chord again and again, not because anyone would notice, but because it sounded right to her own ears.

On exam day, her fingers trembled a little on the first page. She made one small mistake in the middle — a wrong note that hung in the air. Her heart sank.

When results came, she had passed — no distinction. No new medal for the shelf beside her sister's.

Sia waited for the big empty feeling. It came — but smaller than before. She sat at the piano and played the piece again, alone, from start to finish. It sounded fuller than exam day. Her chest felt warm, like the room had more space.

"I still want a medal," she told Amma honestly at dinner.

"And you also love the playing now," Amma smiled, serving rice. "That stays even when the shelf stays the same."

Sia nodded. Effort had become its own quiet prize — one nobody could take off a shelf, but nobody could take away either.

2.title: Slow and Neat

story.title: Neha's Art Project
story.content:
Neha's class was making a giant collage of the ocean. Blue paper, silver foil for fish, cotton for waves — it was the prettiest project of the term, and the teacher would hang the best one in the hallway where the whole school walked every day.

Neha wanted hers to win. She imagined parents stopping to point and whisper, "Look how neat that is." On the first day, she glued fast. Foil stuck to her fingers. Cotton bunched in lumps. Glue smeared across the blue like cloudy water. The ocean looked like a storm had thrown supplies at a board.

"Done!" she announced, breathless, glue strings hanging from her knuckles.

Her partner Ritu peeked over her shoulder. "Maybe we fix the corners? And this fish is upside down."

Neha scowled. "If we slow down, someone else will finish first. Speed is smart."

That afternoon, Neha's Amma watched her wash glue off her hands at the kitchen sink. "You ran like the prize was running away from you."

"It is," Neha said, scrubbing hard.

Amma dried her hands with a soft towel and sat beside her at the table. "Krishna praises action done with a steady mind — not frantic, not lazy. Smart work is calm work. Calm hands see what messy hands miss. Rushing for praise is like building a sand castle while the tide is already coming."

Neha looked at her sticky fingernails and said nothing.

The next day at school, she asked Ritu to help again. "Let's try Amma's way," she admitted.

They laid out all the pieces without gluing first. They stepped back and looked from across the room. They swapped two fish. They trimmed cotton into smaller puffs. They cut neat waves slowly, one strip at a time.

Neha's shoulders unclenched. Her breathing slowed. The board began to look like an ocean you could almost hear — shhh, shhh, against the shore.

On presentation day, another group's collage won the hallway spot. Neha felt a flicker of jealousy in her throat — then she looked at her own work. The corners were straight. The fish gleamed. She could explain every step she and Ritu had taken.

"We can make another one at home," Ritu said, linking arms with her in the corridor.

"Yes," Neha smiled. "Slowly. For us this time."

Calm work had made her proud in a way rushing never had. The prize on the wall mattered less than the quiet skill growing in her hands.

2.title: The Quiet Choice

story.title: Kabir at Recess
story.content:
Recess was loud every day at Kabir's school — balls bouncing, friends calling, games starting and stopping like sudden storms. The playground smelled like dust and mango slices from lunch boxes.

Kabir usually ran toward the first game he saw. If nobody picked him, he felt angry and hot behind his ears. If the game ended early, he complained all the way back to class, kicking at pebbles. His chest often felt tight before the bell rang again, as if he had run a race he never wanted.

One Tuesday, the air was cooler. A new boy stood alone near the neem tree, holding a lunch bag with both hands. Kabir almost ran past toward Vikram's shouting group — then he noticed the boy's shoulders were hunched, like Kabir's felt inside on most days.

At the same moment, Vikram waved hard. "Come! Football! Now! We're one short!"

Kabir's feet wanted to sprint. His mouth wanted to shout, "I'm coming!" But something made him pause on the grass. He breathed in — one, two, three — and out, slow.

He remembered Amma reading from the Gita at bedtime: a person who is steady, whose mind is not pulled like a kite in every wind, finds peace. Calm people choose wisely, not quickly in a fuss.

Kabir walked to the tree instead. "Want to play catch?" he asked the new boy.

The boy looked up, surprised. "I'm Rishi. I don't know the rules here."

"Me neither, sometimes," Kabir laughed. "They change every day."

They played gentle catch with a soft ball from Rishi's bag. Two more kids wandered over and joined without arguing about goals or teams. When the bell rang, Kabir's chest felt light, not tight. Rishi smiled for the first time that day.

In class, Vikram whispered, "Why didn't you come to football? We lost."

"I chose something quieter," Kabir said. "It felt right."

That evening, Kabir wrote in his notebook in big letters: Pause. Breathe. Then choose.

He did not always pick the quiet path. Some days he still ran toward the loudest game. But he had learned that a calm moment could turn a loud fuss into a good day — and that choosing kindly could start a friendship under a tree.

2.title: The Last Biscuit

story.title: Maya and the Cookie Jar
story.content:
Amma had baked butter biscuits that morning before the sun was fully up. The whole house smelled like warmth and sugar. Maya helped decorate three with little chocolate dots — one for her, one for her brother Arun, and one for Appa when he came home tired from the office.

"These are for sharing," Amma said, placing them on the red plate. "Not for gobbling in secret."

Maya nodded, but her tummy rumbled just looking at them.

After school, Maya dropped her bag and ran to the kitchen. Only one biscuit remained on the plate. Arun had gone straight to karate with his friends. Appa was still at work. The lonely biscuit sat golden and perfect in the quiet kitchen, as if it were calling her name in a whisper.

Maya's hand reached out. Her fingers touched the soft edge, still faintly warm from the afternoon sun on the counter. She could eat it in two bites and nobody would know until later — maybe. Her mouth watered.

Then she heard Appa's voice in her head from last week: "Strength is not only muscles. It is also choosing what your senses want right now versus what is fair."

Maya pulled her hand back as if the plate were warm. She closed her eyes and counted five things: the smell of butter, the tick of the clock, the hollow feeling in her hungry tummy, the sight of the red plate, the memory of Arun's karate kick that morning when he almost knocked over her water bottle.

Krishna teaches that wise people can pull their senses back, like a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell — not forever, not harshly, but when grabbing would hurt someone else or break a promise.

Maya took a glass of water instead. She cut an apple into neat slices and ate them slowly at the table, one by one. When Arun burst through the door, sweaty and grinning, she pointed proudly to the plate. "I saved your biscuit."

Arun's face lit up like a lamp. "Really? You didn't eat it? Thanks, Maya!"

When Appa came home, rubbing his neck, Maya gave him his biscuit too. He sat down and ate it with his tea. "That took self-control," he said, ruffling her hair. "Strong heart."

Maya felt taller inside — not because she got praise, but because she had been the kind of sister she wanted to be when nobody was watching.

2.title: The Anger Ladder
2.micro_theme: Angry thoughts grow step by step

story.title: Leo's Bad Afternoon
story.content:
Leo's afternoon started with a stubbed toe on the bed frame — a sharp, silly pain that made him hop on one foot down the hallway. "Ow!" he yelped. It was nobody's fault, but his mood turned prickly like a thorn stuck in his sock.

Downstairs, his little sister Mira was humming a tune from her cartoon while drawing suns with orange crayon. The humming felt too loud in Leo's sore-toe world. "Stop!" he snapped, louder than he meant.

Mira's smile vanished like someone had switched off a light. She hugged her crayons to her chest and went quiet — but her eyes looked wet and wide.

At snack time, Leo reached for the last mango slice on the plate. Mira had saved it with a crayon note: For Leo, love Mira. Appa had cut it specially that morning because Leo loved mango best. Leo was about to eat it when he saw the note. Guilt poked him, but he ate the slice anyway because the day already felt ruined and he did not know how to undo the snap.

Mira cried at the table. Amma came in from her work call, tired lines around her eyes. "What happened here?"

Leo shouted, "Everything! My toe! Her noise! This stupid day!" Words flew out hotter than he meant, bouncing off the kitchen tiles.

That night, Appa sat on Leo's bed and drew a ladder on a piece of paper with four rungs. "Step one: pain — toe hurt. Step two: want — you wanted quiet. Step three: anger — you snapped at Mira. Step four: more anger — shouting at Amma. Krishna shows how desire leads to anger like smoke from a fire. Small sparks become big flames if we feed them."

Leo looked at the ladder. "I didn't mean to make Mira cry."

"I know," Appa said. "Tomorrow, try stopping at step two. Say: I want quiet. Ask kindly. The ladder gets shorter."

The next morning, Leo limped slightly and Mira hummed again over her cereal. Leo felt the snap rising in his chest — but he breathed and said, "Mira, my toe still hurts. Can you hum softer for a bit?"

Mira nodded fast, earnest. "Sorry, Leo. Want a bandage sticker? I have stars."

Leo smiled. The ladder had only two steps today. That felt like a small victory worth keeping.

2.title: Morning Chart

story.title: Rohan's Wind-Down
story.content:
Rohan used to treat bedtime like a surprise party that nobody planned. Sometimes he played games until his eyes burned and the room spun. Sometimes he read one page of a comic and fell asleep with the light on and crumbs on the sheet. Mornings were foggy. He forgot homework. He snapped at his little cousin over cereal because the spoon clinked too loudly.

"I'm tired of being tired," he told Paati on the phone, his voice small.

Paati said, "Come over this weekend. We will make a morning-and-night chart together. Not a punishment — a path to peace."

At Paati's house, they spread chart paper on the dining table and drew two columns with bright markers. Morning: wake, brush, dress, breakfast, pack bag. Night: homework, bath, story, lights out by nine.

"Krishna links a steady, disciplined mind to rest and clarity," Paati explained, stirring tea. "Not rigid like a soldier — gentle like a riverbank that guides water without fighting it."

Rohan chose stickers for each step — stars, moons, little cups of tea. He stuck one star on "brush teeth" right away, grinning.

The first night back home, he wanted to skip bath because a new game level was waiting. Amma did not scold. She pointed to the chart on the fridge. "Check the path. What comes next?"

Rohan groaned, then walked to the bathroom. The warm water quieted his jumpy legs. He read one chapter — not three, not zero. Lights off at nine-fifteen, not midnight.

The next morning was not magic. He still yawned at the bus stop. But he found his maths homework already in the bag because he had packed it the night before. He ate sitting down instead of running with toast in his hand. At school, his teacher looked closer and said, "You look awake today, Rohan."

After one full week with the chart, Rohan noticed something soft inside — less storm, more still pond. Discipline was not a cage. It was a kindly fence around his sleep and his mornings.

He taped a small copy of the chart inside his cupboard door. Peace, he learned, could be built one small step at a time — and that building was a kind of love he gave to himself.

2.title: Monkey Mind Night
2.micro_theme: A restless mind cannot stay happy

story.title: Tina Before the Trip
story.content:
Tina could not sleep. Tomorrow her family was leaving for the hill station — new roads curling like ribbons, a new hotel with a fancy breakfast tray, mist on the windows she had only seen in pictures. Exciting, yes. But her mind was a monkey jumping branch to branch, never resting on one tree.

What if it rains the whole trip? What if she forgets her sweater and shivers? What if the car feels sick on the winding curves? What if she misses her best friend Devika's call and Devika thinks she doesn't care? What if, what if, what if — the questions swung louder than the fan.

She turned left. She turned right. The sheet tangled around her legs like a rope. The clock on the wall ticked louder and louder, as if counting her worries one by one.

Amma knocked softly and slipped in with her dupatta trailing. "Still awake, little monkey?"

Tina groaned into the pillow. "My brain won't sit still. It's too jumpy."

Amma sat on the bed and opened the window a crack. Cool night air slipped in, carrying the smell of jasmine from the garden. "Krishna says a restless mind finds no lasting peace — like a boat tossed without an anchor. We will not fix tomorrow tonight. We will anchor you now."

They tried a game. Amma said, "Name five blue things in this room."

Tina whispered, "Your dupatta… my water bottle cap… part of the rug… Devika's bracelet on the shelf… the cover of my book."

"Good. Now four sounds you can hear."

"Clock. Fan. A dog far away. Your breathing."

"Three slow breaths with me. In through the nose. Out through the mouth."

In, out. In, out. In, out.

Tina's monkey mind still flickered — but it had fewer branches to jump to. Amma's hand on her back was steady, like a riverbank holding water.

"You can be excited and rest," Amma said. "Both are allowed. Tomorrow will arrive whether you spin or sleep."

Tina closed her eyes. She pictured the hill road as a soft ribbon, not a monster. Sleep came in pieces, not all at once, but enough to fill the cup.

In the morning, she packed her sweater without panic and waved at Devika's house on the way out. The monkey was still there sometimes — but she had learned a ladder down from the noisy trees.

2.title: Letting the Balloon Go

story.title: Jay and the Lost Game
story.content:
Jay's chess team had practiced for weeks in the library after school. They knew openings, endgames, and the serious faces you make when you pretend not to be nervous while your knee bounces under the table.

On finals day, Jay played his best game of the year — careful, patient, brave — and still lost on the last move when his opponent's queen slid into a corner he had not seen in time.

He held the feeling like a hot stone in his pocket all weekend. He did not want to eat dal. He snapped when his sister borrowed his charger without asking. He replayed the final move again and again behind his eyes, seeing the queen land like a hammer.

On Monday, Thatha took him to the riverbank after school. The water was brown-green and steady. Children were releasing balloons into the sky — red, blue, yellow — for a local festival, laughing as they let go.

"Hold this," Thatha said, giving Jay a green balloon. Attached was a small paper tag on a string.

"Write one worry you cannot control," Thatha said. "Not the whole tournament — one thread."

Jay wrote in pencil: I can't undo my last move.

He stared at the words until they blurred. His eyes burned, but he did not wipe them quickly. Thatha waited with open hands.

"Krishna teaches that peace grows when we stop clutching every desire and every regret," Thatha said gently. "Like this river — it keeps moving because it does not grab the rocks. Letting go is not giving up on caring. It is making room inside for calm."

Jay tied the tag to the balloon. His fingers trembled. "What if I need to remember to practice harder?"

"You will remember," Thatha said. "Letting go of the hot stone is not dropping your chess board."

Jay released the balloon. It rose, wobbled in the wind, and joined the others — small green courage against the big evening sky.

Jay's chest still felt the loss. But the hot stone feeling loosened, like a fist opening one finger at a time. He breathed in the river smell — mud, water, evening flowers.

That night he set up the chess board again at the dining table. He cared. He practiced. But he did not carry the whole weekend storm in his pocket anymore.

Peace, he learned, sometimes looks like open hands.

3.title: Show, Don't Only Tell

story.title: Anika Picks Up the Paper
story.content: One ordinary school day became special for Anika. The story is called "Anika Picks Up the Paper." Anika felt stuck—a small choice felt very big. Friends argued, or a test felt scary, or someone needed help and Anika wanted to walk away. Then Anika remembered what Krishna teaches in the Gita: Show, Don't Only Tell. Anika took a deep breath, spoke kindly, and did the right thing even when it was not the easy way. That night, Anika felt proud—not because everyone clapped, but because the heart felt quiet and good.

10.title: Goodness All Around

story.title: Stars in Many Skills
story.content: One ordinary school day became special for Dev. The story is called "Stars in Many Skills." Dev felt stuck—a small choice felt very big. Friends argued, or a test felt scary, or someone needed help and Dev wanted to walk away. Then Dev remembered what Krishna teaches in the Gita: Goodness All Around. story.title: The Courage to Tell Truth
story.content: One ordinary school day became special for Riya. The story is called "The Courage to Tell Truth." Riya felt stuck—a small choice felt very big. Friends argued, or a test felt scary, or someone needed help and Riya wanted to walk away. Then Riya remembered what Krishna teaches in the Gita: Growing Good Qualities. Riya took a deep breath, spoke kindly, and did the right thing even when it was not the easy way. That night, Riya felt proud—not because everyone clapped, but because the heart felt quiet and good.

Riya చిక్కులో పడింది—చిన్న ఎంపిక చాలా పెద్దదిగా అనిపించింది. స్నేహితులు గొడవ పడ్డారు, లేదా పరీక్ష భయంగా ఉంది, లేదా ఎవరికైనా సహాయం కావాలి కానీ Riya దూరంగా వెళ్లాలనుకున్నాడు. అప్పుడు గీతలో కృష్ణుడు బోధించిన మంచి గుణాలు పెంపడం గుర్తుకు వచ్చింది.
